newsitem.title: FRANCE: World Cup promotions kick off early in France.
newsitem.headline: World Cup promotions kick off early in France.

text.p: France has football fever 10 months before it hosts the World Cup tournament next June, and advertisers linked with the event are getting in early on the act.
Oil firm Total, the offical oil company for the World Cup, has set out to be the first with World Cup clothes and accessories on sale, said Alain Castinel, Total's head of advertising and promotion.
Its World cup T-shirts and footballs have been available in its service stations for purchase for a small sum together with a full tank of gasoline from the beginning of July.
It is also selling a World Cup baseball cap and a soft toy version of Footix the rooster, the tournament's mascot.
"We thought World Cup products would be everywhere from the end of the summer holidays, and we thought it would be clever to start earlier," Castinel said.
Total is a minor World Cup partner, with no panels in the stadiums, so it sought visibility by being first off the mark, he said.

Total's advertising agency CLM/BBDO is running radio spots at weekends until the end of August with the voice of Guy Roux, the boss of Auxerre football club and one of the better-known French football managers.
It has just finished a week-long billboard campaign for the peak of holiday travel across France, showing the T-shirt and football with humorous slogans.
Castinel declined to give the budget for Total's World Cup promotions, but said the company was not spending beyond its usual annual advertising campaign or service station gift budgets.

As the summer holidays end the French will be able to buy a range of sports and leisurewear bearing the logo of Stade de France, the consortium building the stadium near Paris which will host the tournament's final.

The consortium aims to generate extra cash by merchandising Stade de France items, in the same way as tennis venues Roland Garros and Wimbeldon and Wembley Stadium have done, said Stade de France's programming and development manager Jean-Christophe Giletta.
"People are doing more and more merchandising... in France we are behind for this type of product," he said.

Stade de France clothes -- which the consortium hopes will be followed by own-label key rings, ties and watches -- is not inspired by the World Cup, but rather by the example of other stadiums and demand from visitors and shops, Giletta said.
"We really felt a very strong demand for Stade de France products," he said.

The consortium expects merchandising turnover of eight to 10 million francs ($1.6 million) a year, with no dip after the World Cup is over, as the stadium will be hosting other major events which will generate interest in its own-label products, he said.
French building firms Bouygues, GTM Entrepose and SGE are financing 52 percent of the 2.6 billion franc cost of building the Stade de France stadium.
